title: Cross-region KV serialization & tail latency exploration - Sable Systems
summary: Deep dive with Sable Systems on unexplained p99 spikes when serving long-context responses across regions. Focus on how cross-region KV serialization, VPC peering paths, and recent quantization experiments could be amplifying tail latency. Agreed to run targeted microbenchmarks and provide topology-aware configuration suggestions; Redwood to share quantization profile effects and a test harness for KV serialization checks.
action_items: Meera Shah: run cross-region KV serialization microbenchmark (p95/p99) and share raw logs - due 2027-01-25
Tom Alvarez: capture iperf/traceroute during a p99 event and upload to shared folder - due 2027-01-22
Daniel Ortiz: produce simplified topology diagram showing VPC peering paths / NAT gateways and annotate our suggested fallback route - due 2027-01-24
Priya Nair: provide representative prompt sets and a few failing convo ids for regression analysis - due 2027-01-21
next_steps: Redwood to deliver a benchmarking harness (KV serialization + small model) for Sable to run in their VPC
Schedule a follow-up 30-minute sync next week to review microbenchmark results
Share a short note on quantization profiles that avoid excessive CPU kernel fallbacks
transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2027-01-18
Time: 16:00 PST
Duration: 38 minutes
Attendees: Alex Park (Redwood AE), Meera Shah (Redwood SE), Daniel Ortiz (Redwood SRE), Priya Nair (Sable Head of ML), Tom Alvarez (Sable Infra Lead), Hannah Li (Sable Platform Eng)

Auto-summary: brief run-through of p99 spikes, focus on cross-region KV serialization, streaming vs non-streaming behavior, and quantization side-effects.

[00:00] Alex Park: hey everyone, thanks for blocking time. quick agenda — Meera will walk through the runtime traces we collected, then we want to pair that with what Sable is seeing in their VPC. goal is figure out why p99s spike during long responses across regions.

[00:18] Priya Nair: thanks Alex. yeah we've seen these spike windows, usually when context goes beyond 3k tokens and when requests cross from us-east to eu-west. sometimes it's steady, sometimes it's like a microburst.

[00:33] Meera Shah: ok great, so we pulled three representative traces. one thing to flag up front — our trace labels sometimes call the cache step K-V serialization or "K V serial" in the logs; there may be mismatches with your telemetry naming.

[00:50] Tom Alvarez: yep we noticed different naming across teams, that made correlation harder. also, we have peered VPCs with a transit VPC and a NAT in the path for some regions, which could add asymmetric hops.

[01:05] Meera Shah: cool. so first heatmap — p95 is pretty stable but p99 jumps when the request touches the KV cache and then has to serialize/deserialize across the wire to a remote replica. the deserialization step is sometimes CPU-bound on the requester side, which causes backpressure into the runtime.

[01:30] Hannah Li: when you say deserialization, is that protobuf, msgpack, json? we've got some legacy pipelines using JSON for the KV payloads.

[01:40] Meera Shah: good question. in Redwood's default path we use a compact binary protobuf blob. but when the customer-side agent falls back (their shim) it was using json in some older regions — so that's a big difference. json + large kv payloads hits CPU and serialization latency.

[01:58] Priya Nair: hmm that might explain it. we did an experiment last month with our shim and saw CPU ramp on the host that was requesting the KV entries.

[02:10] Daniel Ortiz: another dimension — quantization. when models are quantized we sometimes route to a different execution kernel that changes the CPU/GPU interplay. those kernels can yield more frequent context cache misses and slightly bigger KV payloads because of altered key formats. i've seen a 3-5% percent increase in median but it can amplify the tail if coupled with network jitter.

[02:36] Tom Alvarez: wait, so quantization affects the KV format? i thought it only changed tensor sizes.

[02:44] Meera Shah: normally quantization shouldn't change logical keys, but our adaptive runtime sometimes stores a small header per cache entry when using certain quantized layouts to accelerate lookup. it's an experiment that trades a few extra bytes for faster deserialization on the hot path, but in cross-region transfers those extra bytes plus json fallback can add latency.

[03:05] Priya Nair: that matches our window where the p99 only appears for quantized model variant serving. non-quantized runs didn't show the same spike.

[03:15] Alex Park: ok so preliminary hypothesis — cross-region KV transfers, combined with mismatched serialization formats plus kernel fallbacks tied to quantization, are increasing p99. next, streaming vs non-streaming — did we see different behavior there?

[03:30] Meera Shah: yes. streaming keeps the KV hot path on the serving side for longer and amortizes some CPU costs across token emission. for very long responses streaming tends to help median and often p95. but if there's a mid-stream serialization hiccup — for example an RPC retry — the tail can be worse because the connection is already elevated. non-streaming (full-response) has a single critical path: if serialization step blocks early, the whole response is delayed but we sometimes avoid repeated small RPCs that are sensitive to network jitter.

[04:05] Hannah Li: so there's a tradeoff — streaming reduces average latency for long answers but increases sensitivity to intermittent network errors mid-stream.

[04:15] Tom Alvarez: can you elaborate on the RPC retry you mentioned? we have gRPC with our own retry policy, might be interacting oddly.

[04:24] Meera Shah: in a streaming scenario, if the KV RPC to the remote replica times out and then the runtime retries, the token stream stalls until the retry completes. depending on the backoff policy it can be a few hundred ms to multiple seconds. in non-streaming we either fail fast or block the entire call, which looks worse but at least behavior is consistent.

[04:48] Daniel Ortiz: adding to that, our topology-aware routing can fall back to a local compressed cache. but that requires a cache warm path; if it's cold and we attempt remote fetches the retries can cascade. we've seen a pattern where multiple concurrent requests hit the same hotkey and create a surge — a classic hot-shard problem.

[05:10] Priya Nair: that hotkey scenario is exactly what we saw this morning — a short window with many concurrent requests to the same doc id. did you find any soft limits we can tweak?

[05:20] Meera Shah: yes — batching window size and per-key queue depth are two levers. increasing batch window slightly can allow more efficient serialization and fewer RPCs, but it increases median latency for small requests. queue depth controls how many in-flight requests wait for a hotkey; setting it too high creates head-of-line blocking.

[05:45] Tom Alvarez: what about TCP settings or keepalive? could frequent connection churn be hurting us across the peered link?

[05:52] Daniel Ortiz: definitely. we recommend longer keepalive for long-lived streaming connections, enable TCP_NODELAY carefully (sometimes it's harmful), and tune socket buffers to match your bandwidth-delay product across inter-region links. also ensure the MTU isn't being fragmented by some transit device.

[06:15] Hannah Li: we use a transit VPC provider that may fragment at certain hops — we'll add MTU checks.

[06:21] Alex Park: back to quantization — Meera mentioned kernel fallbacks. can you explain how a quantization profile could cause a CPU kernel to trigger and increase latency?

[06:31] Meera Shah: sure. certain int8 kernels are fast on newer GPUs but on older or mixed nodes the runtime sometimes executes a fallback path that runs partly on CPU or uses a slower generic kernel. That fallback increases both deserialization and inference time. When that lines up with a remote KV fetch it's a multiplier for tail latency.

[06:52] Priya Nair: is there a way to highlight those fallback events in the trace? our observability shows a generic spike but not the kernel reason.

[06:58] Daniel Ortiz: we can add a small tag to the trace export that indicates kernel type and quantization profile used. Meera can include that in the microbenchmark outputs.

[07:10] Meera Shah: yep we'll include kernel annotations. also we'll surface whether the runtime had to recompile kernels at runtime which can happen if it decides a different codepath is more optimal for a particular input shape — that even triggers short compilation stalls.

[07:28] Tom Alvarez: recompile at runtime — that's a big red flag for us in production. can it be disabled?

[07:34] Meera Shah: yes, we have a "compile-on-start" option that precompiles a model for a given sequence length distribution. for production you'd want to enable that and pin the profile. otherwise we do lazy compilation which reduces startup cost but can surface as small stalls.

[07:50] Priya Nair: do you have advice for sequence length settings? our mix is 512-6k tokens with a heavy tail toward 2.5k.

[07:58] Meera Shah: recommend precompiles for 512, 2048, 4096 and a catchall 6k. choose profiles based on your percentile distribution; compile-on-start for the top three reduces mid-request surprises.

[08:12] Alex Park: let's talk about concrete tests — Meera, can you outline the microbench harness you propose?

[08:18] Meera Shah: sure. small harness — three parts: 1) synthetic KV serialization loop that mimics your key sizes and payloads across protobuf vs json vs msgpack; 2) a model-run with representative prompts comparing quantized vs FP16 models with precompiled kernels; 3) network emulation across peered path (latency/jitter) to simulate cross-region. outputs: p50/p95/p99 and kernel annotations, plus flame events for serialization.

[08:45] Tom Alvarez: if we run that in our VPC what should we expect in terms of resource usage? will it blow up our infra?

[08:53] Meera Shah: it's lightweight, a small worker that simulates concurrent clients. you should provision a test node with similar NIC and CPU to your production frontends. concurrency knobs let you push it without affecting prod.

[09:06] Hannah Li: will you provide the harness as a container? we prefer that for quick runs in our staging VPC.

[09:11] Meera Shah: yes, we'll share a docker image and a terraform snippet to spin up the test instance in a sanitized subnet.

[09:20] Priya Nair: on the sizing side, we also want to know if certain quantization profiles should be avoided in cross-region setups. is that a thing?

[09:28] Daniel Ortiz: yeah some aggressive int4/int3 profiles assume very low-latency local storage and certain kernel support; they can be brittle across mixed hardware and add small metadata per entry which when compounded increases payload. not all workloads benefit; our recommendation is to benchmark quantization profiles with your distribution and prefer conservative profiles for cross-region fallbacks.

[09:52] Tom Alvarez: could Redwood route requests preferentially to local replicas to avoid cross-region fetches? we don't want single-region capacity to be overwhelmed though.

[10:00] Meera Shah: we have topology-aware routing: prefer local replica, fallback to remote if TTL or local misses. we can set stronger locality policies for certain tenant IDs or routes. that reduces cross-region fetches but does require sufficient capacity locally or controlled fallbacks to alternate model variants.

[10:18] Priya Nair: that's promising. what about batching settings? you mentioned increasing batch windows could help. any concrete starting values?

[10:26] Meera Shah: start with a 5-10ms batch window for your steady traffic and test 20-30ms for heavy long-context flows; monitor p50/p95. also use dynamic batching thresholds — like process small batches immediately but wait up to X ms if tokens are likely to be coalesced. that tends to smooth serialization calls.

[10:47] Hannah Li: any cautions on enabling dynamic batching in streaming?

[10:52] Meera Shah: yes, dynamic batching in streaming must avoid buffering the first token too long — we provide a "first-token-priority" override so streaming responses don't feel sluggish. it's in our runtime config.

[11:05] Alex Park: switching gears briefly — can you recap how to detect hotkeys? we want automation to alert earlier.

[11:12] Daniel Ortiz: hotkeys show up as a small set of keys with huge QPS and queue depth. set alert when per-key queue length crosses threshold and when p99 for that key diverges from global p99 by a factor. also instrument histogram per-key.

[11:28] Priya Nair: can Redwood's console show per-key histograms?

[11:33] Meera Shah: yes we can surface that, but there's privacy/ingestion cost tradeoff. we recommend sampling and only indexing hotkey candidates. we'll share a dashboard template.

[11:44] Tom Alvarez: about VPC peering — could asymmetric routing create scenarios where seq of hops goes via a third region intermittently? we saw that in traceroutes before.

[11:53] Daniel Ortiz: yes, BGP path changes and transit provider policies can create transient asymmetric hops. that increases jitter and sometimes causes out-of-order packet arrival which hurts retransmission. that's why we suggested running tcpdump and traceroute during a p99 window.

[12:08] Priya Nair: ok we'll schedule that during our next expected spike window.

[12:14] Alex Park: any other low-hanging configuration changes Sable can try immediately?

[12:18] Meera Shah: three quick ones: enforce protobuf serialization on the shim, enable compile-on-start for common profiles, increase keepalive and tune socket buffers. those three often knock down many p99s.

[12:30] Hannah Li: protobuf enforcement sounds straightforward; i'll push a change to the shim in staging and report back.

[12:36] Tom Alvarez: i'll run an MTU and traceroute sweep and attach to the ticket.

[12:41] Alex Park: great. let's capture the follow-ups — Meera will send the harness, Daniel will add kernel annotations to traces, Tom and Hannah will collect network artifacts, Priya will share prompt sets.

[12:55] Priya Nair: one last question — what's Redwood's recommendation on fallbacks when local capacity is thin? do you prefer using a lower-cost quantized variant or routing cross-region?

[13:04] Meera Shah: depends on your SLA. if tail latency is critical prefer local lower-quality variant with deterministic behavior. if quality is critical, accept cross-region routing but with a circuit-breaker that falls back to a cheap cached summary at a bounded latency. we can help you test both patterns.

[13:24] Tom Alvarez: what's the typical latency hit for cross-region routing vs local quantized? just ballpark numbers?

[13:30] Meera Shah: ballpark: local quantized variant might add 10-40ms overhead (kernel dependent), cross-region fetch can add 50-200ms depending on hop and jitter. in worst-case with retries we've seen seconds, which is why we want retries tuned.

[13:48] Alex Park: ok excellent. wrapping up — action items and next steps as we outlined. thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the harness and a 30-minute sync next Tue.

[14:02] Priya Nair: thanks all, helpful session.

End of transcript
